handbookNote: Pennsylvania Real Estate Broker license exam, administered by Pearson VUE under contract with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission (Department of State, Bureau of Professional and Occupational Affairs). IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE ORIGINAL BUILD BRIEF: the brief assumed PSI is the current vendor and cited '63 P.S. Section 455.902' as the escrow provision. Neither is correct as of this build (2026-08-30) -- PSI Exams stopped registering/administering Pennsylvania real estate candidates as of April 1, 2023 (confirmed via the PA Real Estate Commission's own Announcements page on pa.gov), and Pearson VUE has been the exam vendor since that transition, confirmed both by that same PA-government announcement and by Pearson VUE's own March 2026 Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission Candidate Handbook (#093900, rev. 03/2026), which was fetched directly and extracted via pdftotext for this build. Section 455.902 of RELRA is actually the Act's 'Effective date' section (confirmed via the full statutory table of contents fetched from legis.state.pa.us) -- the real escrow/trust-fund-handling provision is RELRA Section 608.5 ('Handling of deposits and other escrows'), 63 P.S. Section 455.608.5, added by the act of July 6, 2009 (P.L.58, No.14), which this bank cites throughout instead. Exam mechanics were CONFIRMED directly from the official Pearson VUE candidate handbook's 'Available Exams and Time Allotted' table and the separate PSI-superseding 'Pennsylvania Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline' (effective March 16, 2026) and 'National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers' (effective April 1, 2025), both bundled in the same handbook PDF: the broker exam is split into a National portion (80 scored items, 5-10 unscored pretest items, 150 minutes, 75% passing) and a Pennsylvania State-specific portion (40 scored items, up to 10 unscored pretest items, 60 minutes, 75% passing), for a combined 120 scored items and 210 minutes (3.5 hours) if both are taken; fees are $52 (national) and $49 (state-specific), with a same-order combination discount; passing results are valid 3 years; broker exam authorization (after completing the first required education course) is valid 10 years, versus 5 years for salespersons. Licensure prerequisites -- 21 years old, high school graduate/equivalent, at least 3 years' experience as a licensed salesperson (or Commission-deemed equivalent), and 240 hours (16 credits) of professional real estate education -- were CONFIRMED both from RELRA Section 511 (63 P.S. Section 455.511) and from 49 Pa. Code Section 35.271, which was fetched in full verbatim text (via direct HTML fetch converted with a Python script, since WebFetch's summarization truncated it) and which also gave the exact broker-education-credit breakdown: 2 credits in a Commission-approved real estate LAW course, 2 credits in a Commission-approved OFFICE MANAGEMENT course, at least 6 of the remaining 12 credits from 3+ specifically enumerated subjects (finance, investment, property management, valuation, etc.), and the final 6 credits from any real estate course -- CORRECTING an earlier, less-precise secondary-source claim (found via initial web search) of a '200-point experience chart' loosely modeled on other states' broker banks in this project; that 200-point/chart claim does NOT appear anywhere in RELRA or 49 Pa. Code Section 35.271's actual text and was discarded rather than used. Real statute/regulation citations used throughout, independently verified via legis.state.pa.us (full RELRA text fetched and converted to plain text), pacodeandbulletin.gov (49 Pa. Code Chapter 35 sections fetched individually as raw HTML and converted to text), and pa.gov, include: RELRA (63 P.S. Sections 455.101-455.902) Sections 511-513 (broker qualifications/application/entity licensing), 521-522 (salesperson, for comparison), 601-610 (broker/salesperson duties, prohibited acts, agency-relationship duties 606.1-606.6, initial-interview disclosure 608 and its rental-only 'Consumer Notice' carve-out, written-agreement disclosures 608.1, mandatory sales-contract disclosures 608.2 including the zoning-classification/HOP disclosures, CMA disclosure 608.3, escrow handling 608.5, broker price opinions 608.6, time-share/campground 5-day cancellation right 609, wholesale-transaction 30-day cancellation right 610), 701-702 (Commission hearings and the actual-knowledge/imputed-knowledge standard limiting vicarious license discipline), 801-803 (Real Estate Recovery Fund: $10 per-license funding fee, $300k/$500k fund-balance thresholds, $20,000 per-claim/$100,000 per-licensee caps, automatic license suspension on fund payment), 301-305 (unlicensed practice civil/criminal penalties and exclusions), and 404.1 (14-hour biennial continuing education, 5-year inactive-license window); 49 Pa. Code Chapter 35 Sections 35.201 (definitions, including 'associate broker' and 'broker of record'), 35.242-35.246 (office/branch office/supervision/license display/inspection), 35.251-35.255 (status of licensure -- relicensure, deceased/incapacitated broker substitution, reciprocal licenses), 35.271 (broker exam qualification and education-credit breakdown, fetched and quoted in full, including the Bhala v. State Real Estate Commission, 617 A.2d 841 (Pa. Cmwlth. 1992) case note), 35.284/35.286/35.287 (consumer-relationship disclosures, records retention, supervised property management by salespersons), and 35.321/35.323/35.324/35.325 (the OLDER 1989-vintage escrow regulations, which still coexist alongside and are cross-referenced by RELRA's newer 2009 Section 608.5 escrow statute -- both are cited in this bank since both remain independently in force). Pennsylvania-specific consumer-protection statutes outside RELRA, independently verified via primary-source PDF/HTML fetches, include: the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law, 68 Pa.C.S. Sections 7301-7315 (part of the broader Residential Real Estate Transfers Law, 68 Pa.C.S. Sections 7101-7512, which also includes the separate Home Inspection Law at Sections 7501-7513) -- fetched and quoted in detail including its exemption list, disclosure-form content list, and the notably narrower actual-knowledge liability standard for AGENTS (Section 7310) versus sellers (Section 7308-7309); the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act, 43 P.S. Sections 951-963 (housing discrimination at Section 955(h), blockbusting at Section 955.3, and the local-only Philadelphia Fair Practices Ordinance source-of-income protection, which is flagged as a CITY ordinance, not a statewide PHRA protection); the Landlord and Tenant Act of 1951, 68 P.S. Section 250.101 et seq. (security deposit caps of 2 months' rent in year one/1 month thereafter under Section 250.511a, the 2-year/$100 interest-escrow trigger under Section 250.511b, the 30-day itemized-deduction/double-damages remedy under Section 250.512, and the 10/15/30-day notice-to-quit tiers under Section 250.501); the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, 53 P.S. Section 10101 et seq. (statewide zoning enabling act, inapplicable to home-rule Philadelphia and Pittsburgh); the Uniform Planned Community Act, 68 Pa.C.S. Sections 5101-5414; the Loan Interest and Protection Law ('Act 6'), 41 P.S. Section 101 et seq.; the Radon Certification Act, 63 P.S. Sections 2001-2014; and Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax, 72 P.S. Section 8102-C (1% state rate, confirmed via the pa.gov Department of Revenue's own Realty Transfer Tax page), including its Common Level Ratio (CLR) mechanism used in both assessment appeals and certain transfer-tax valuations. Some content -- the Act 91/HEMAP foreclosure-notice process, the exact PHRA owner-occupied ('two-unit') and religious-organization exemptions, net listing's legal status in Pennsylvania, spot zoning case law, the SALDO/PRD land-use tools, Pennsylvania's inheritance tax rate tiers, and Clean and Green's roll-back-tax mechanics -- is flagged in-content with 'hedge: well-corroborated...' source_note language because it rests on well-corroborated secondary/practitioner sources (county government pages, established real-estate-law firms, state-agency program pages) rather than a pinpoint-cited primary statutory subsection independently fetched in this research pass; this follows the same grounding-transparency standard used in the ny_re_broker bank. Standard national real-estate content not tied to a specific Pennsylvania statute (appraisal theory, general contract-law doctrine, federal RESPA/TILA/ECOA/Fair Housing Act history, real estate math formulas, MACRS depreciation periods, mortgage-clause definitions) is grounded directly against the Pearson VUE National/General Exam Content Outline for Brokers (effective April 1, 2025) -- fetched and read in full from the same official candidate-handbook PDF -- and flagged 'hedge: standard...' where the underlying doctrine is federal or industry-standard rather than Pennsylvania statutory law, consistent with this project's grounding standard. Per the user's brief that broker content should go substantially deeper than a generic salesperson bank into broker-specific supervision, escrow, and office-management territory, this 282-question bank concentrates 103 of its 282 questions (about 36.5%) into six broker-specific buckets: Broker Licensure Requirements & Application, Broker Office Management/Branch Offices/Recordkeeping, Broker Supervision of Salespersons & Associate Brokers, Escrow & Trust Fund Management, Commission/Compensation & Broker-Salesperson Relationships, and License Law/Commission Discipline/Recovery Fund -- content that a PA salesperson-tier bank would not need to cover in this depth. On the brief's specific judgment-call questions: (1) Pennsylvania does NOT have a separate 'associate broker' EXAM -- an associate broker (defined at 49 Pa. Code Section 35.201 simply as 'an individual broker who is employed by another broker') and a standard/independent broker both take and pass the identical Broker Examination described above; the distinction is about who the broker chooses to work under after licensure, not a different licensing track, so this bank's content targets the single Broker Examination that qualifies a candidate for either arrangement -- directly analogous to how the ny_re_broker bank treats NY's associate broker concept. (2) Pearson VUE's PA content outline DOES cleanly separate national (80-item, federal/generic) and state-specific (40-item, PA-statute-and-regulation) sections with published item-count subtotals per major topic and cognitive-level (knowledge/application/analysis) breakdowns for the national portion -- this bank's bucket structure loosely tracks that split, weighting PA-statute-grounded buckets (01-09, 14, 16-18) more heavily than the more generically national buckets (10-13, 15) in proportion to their real-world tested weight. (3) Pennsylvania is NOT a mandatory-attorney closing state like New York, nor a pure title-company state -- it sits in between, with attorney involvement common but not legally required, and with meaningful regional variation (heavier attorney involvement in Philadelphia and parts of western PA/Pittsburgh); this bank's Closing/Settlement bucket presents that nuance rather than assuming either extreme, and separately flags Pennsylvania's classification as a 'wet funding' state (same-day/near-same-day loan disbursement) as a well-corroborated market convention rather than a codified 'Wet Settlement Act' (that specific statute name belongs to Virginia, not Pennsylvania, per this research pass -- a correction to the brief's implicit assumption). Price set at $29.99 (2999 cents) to match this project's standardized going rate for Real Estate tracks, consistent with ny_re_broker.json, ca_re_broker.json, tx_re_broker.json, and fl_re_broker.json. Answer choices were drafted correct-as-choice_a throughout, then deterministically rotated into final A/B/C/D position via scripts/tracks/rotate_pa_re_broker_answers.js (global sequential-cycle rotation across all questions in file order, not manual), yielding a final distribution of A: 71 (25.2%), B: 71 (25.2%), C: 70 (24.8%), D: 70 (24.8%) across all 282 questions.
